transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-20
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~48 mins
Attendees: Ethan Cole (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Orion Head of ML), Leah Martinez (Orion Platform Eng), Samir Patel (CTO)

Summary:
Quick discovery on reliability and incident tolerance for Orion's planned LLM-powered recommendations service. Focus on fallbacks, multi-region routing, and SLA levels for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployments. Agreed to run a POC and exchange SLA/security docs.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Ethan Cole: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros, I'm Ethan, I'm the AE here at Redwood.
[00:12] Daniel Park: Hey Ethan, Daniel here, head of ML at Orion. We've got Leah and Samir with us.
[00:18] Leah Martinez: Hi all.
[00:20] Priya Nair: Priya, Redwood SE - I'll mainly run through the technical parts.
[00:25] Samir Patel: Samir, CTO. We're evaluating reliability and incident tolerance, mostly around fallbacks and multi-region.
[00:33] Ethan Cole: Great, so high level, we're trying to understand your SLOs, traffic patterns, and what failure modes you're worried about. Daniel, can you share where you're at today?
[00:44] Daniel Park: Sure. We run our recommender in prod for web and mobile, currently calling a mix of in-house models and OpenAI via API. Baseline p95 is ~120ms for simple text gen requests, p99 around 720ms during peaks. Peak QPS is 900 for the 2pm ET window, long tail spikes up to ~1.6k for promos.
[01:05] Leah Martinez: We want under 200ms p95 for the new feature, and pretty strict availability - close to five 9s for core checkout flows, but for recs we can tolerate brief fallbacks.
[01:18] Ethan Cole: Good context. When you say fallback - what does that look like? Simpler model, cached responses, or degrade to a non-LLM rule-based response?
[01:28] Daniel Park: Preferably cached responses for repeated queries, otherwise auto-fallback to a smaller, cheaper model. Worst case, we have a deterministic rule engine.
[01:38] Priya Nair: That's aligned with what Redwood supports - we do prefix/KV cache + automated fallback policies to compatible model variants. Our routing can fail over by policy: latency-first, cost-first, or region affinity.
[01:50] Samir Patel: Can you explain the region failover? If a region goes down, how quickly can traffic shift to another region without auth or data issues?
[02:02] Priya Nair: Two parts: control plane and data plane. For Hosted our control plane is global; we have multi-region serving. We can route by region with automatic health checks; typical TTL is seconds for detecting unhealthy endpoints, then traffic shifts to a warm standby region. For Dedicated we provide reserved pools in the target regions and can configure cross-region fallback. For Private (VPC/on-prem), it's up to the customer network config but we provide a runbook and routing primitives.
[02:32] Leah Martinez: What about state - KV cache and session tokens? If we fail over, do we lose cache and cold start latency will spike?
[02:40] Priya Nair: Short answer: yes, cache locality matters. We do prefix/KV cache replication strategies; for strict consistency you'd want shared cache in a replicated store. For most use cases, we accept some cold starts and mitigate via warm standby and KV cache shipping. We'll share our multi-region cache doc.
[02:55] Daniel Park: Are there examples of fallback to cheaper model variants automatically? We worry about hallucination changes between variants.
[03:03] Priya Nair: Yes - you can define compatible model groups and fidelity tiers. In an incident, policy can route to a medium-fidelity variant with lower token cost. You can tie routing to quality gates and safeties - e.g., if a regression on evals is detected, don't fallback. We log these events for postmortem.
[03:20] Samir Patel: SLA talk - we need clarity. For Hosted what SLAs do you offer, and how do they differ from Dedicated?
[03:28] Ethan Cole: Hosted tiers have published uptime and latency SLOs - for paid hosted plans we can discuss 99.9% monthly availability and p95 latency targets depending on model class. Dedicated comes with contract-backed SLAs with higher commit (e.g., 99.95 to 99.99) depending on reserved capacity and runbook. For Private deployments we typically provide platform support SLAs but network/infra is customer-managed, so some parts are shared responsibility. We'll send the exact SLA doc.
[03:52] Leah Martinez: What's the penalty or credit model for SLA misses?
[03:55] Ethan Cole: Standard credit-based model in the SLA doc - credits scale with length and severity of downtime. We'll attach the SLA excerpt in follow-up.
[04:03] Daniel Park: On the incident tolerance side - how do you handle unexpected model-serving regressions? For example, a quantization regresses quality overnight.
[04:12] Priya Nair: We recommend canary rollouts and automatic rollback policies. Redwood Optimize can surface quantization recommendations and flag quality regressions against your eval sets. If a regression is detected, an automated rollback to last-good variant plus alerting occurs. We also support manual canary promotion.
[04:29] Samir Patel: Can we run a POC to stress test failover and fallback? We'd like to see p99 under load across regions.
[04:36] Ethan Cole: Absolutely - typical POC: dedicated warm pool in two regions, synthetic traffic profiles, and we intentionally inject failover to observe latency and error behavior. Priya will own the test plan.
[04:47] Priya Nair: I'll propose a plan: baseline run, regional failure simulation, model-fallback test, and cache sync test. We'll produce charts for p50/p95/p99 and token cost delta when falling back.
[04:58] Leah Martinez: Security question - if we use Dedicated or Private, can you integrate with our KMS and do envelope encryption? We need audit logs for all token-level actions.
[05:07] Priya Nair: Yes, Dedicated and Private support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, customer-managed HSM). We emit detailed audit logs; retention and access controls are configurable. We'll share SOC2 and encryption docs.
[05:18] Daniel Park: One nit - sometimes product names get mangled in transcripts, so apologies if I say "k v cash" earlier - we mean KV cache.
[05:25] Ethan Cole: No worries. Another operational piece - runbooks and playbooks. We provide sample runbooks for common incidents (regional outage, model corruption, high latency) and can co-author for your team.
[05:36] Samir Patel: How about routing decisions - can we do split by tenant or route based on customer tiers? For example, premium users route to dedicated region pool.
[05:45] Priya Nair: Yes, routing policies support tenant-aware routing, traffic weights, and canary tags. You can set route rules: if header X-Priority=gold then route to Dedicated pool in region A, else hosted region B.
[05:58] Leah Martinez: Any limitations on model compatibility for fallback? If our main model is a custom finetune, can fallback use an open checkpoint?
[06:05] Priya Nair: You can define compatible fallbacks ahead of time. If your custom finetune depends on specific tokenizer changes, fallback to a base checkpoint may change outputs; we recommend evaluation suites to quantify differences. During POC we'll include a quality regression matrix.
[06:20] Daniel Park: Sounds good. On billing - if we failover to another region, does that incur cross-region egress or extra charges?
[06:28] Ethan Cole: For Hosted, billing is per-token with region tagging; cross-region egress is minimal for API responses but there may be data transfer costs if you replicate large caches and logs. For Dedicated, we can structure pricing to include reserved cross-region capacity. We'll map cost delta during the POC.
[06:44] Samir Patel: Who owns post-incident postmortem? If Redwood's runtime had a kernel-level bug, do you lead the incident review?
[06:52] Priya Nair: For Hosted or Dedicated with our managed services, Redwood ops will participate in the postmortem and own runtime fixes; for Private, we collaborate and provide artifacts but customer infra ownership shifts some responsibilities. We'll include escalation contacts in the runbook.
[07:06] Daniel Park: Any references you can send now?
[07:09] Ethan Cole: I'll send the Dedicated pricing + SLA doc and the hosted reliability FAQ. Priya will share the routing/fallback diagrams and sample runbook. Links: https://redwood.ai/docs/sla (SLA extract), https://redwood.ai/docs/multi-region-routing (diagram), https://redwood.ai/docs/fallback-policies (examples).
[07:27] Leah Martinez: Great. Timeline - if the POC week of 5/27 works, we need anything from our infra side?
[07:35] Priya Nair: We'll need a service account for perf testing, and an IP allowlist for Dedicated pools. If Private, we'll need network peering info. We'll produce a checklist.
[07:45] Daniel Park: Ok, last question: what's typical failover detection latency? Seconds? Minutes?
[07:51] Priya Nair: Health checks detect failures in ~10-30s usually, then we shift traffic; cold starts add 100-500ms depending on model and cache locality. Warm standby tuning can reduce that a lot.
[08:04] Samir Patel: That helps.
[08:07] Ethan Cole: Cool - recap and next steps in chat then we'll follow up with the docs.
[08:12] Priya Nair: I'll kick off the POC plan doc after the call.
[08:15] Daniel Park: Thanks all, talk soon.

--- End transcript ---

Notes: Transcript has occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "k v cash" for KV cache). Customer prioritized p95 latency under 200ms for feature, interested in Dedicated warm pools plus Hosted for burst. POC scope agreed: two-region dedicated warm pool, synthetic traffic, simulated region failure, model-fallback scenarios, and quality checks.

References shared during call (to be attached in follow-up): https://redwood.ai/docs/sla , https://redwood.ai/docs/multi-region-routing , https://redwood.ai/docs/fallback-policies
